turns.content: I’m Felix — I run a small pathology lab subleasing from MedVance Holdings for $8,500 a month. Section 8.3 of our lease caps late fees at a one-time, non-compounding 5%, but their accounting coordinator just sent me a $14,200 demand built by compounding 5% monthly across trailing balances, and a 5-day notice to cure default. I have the contract text and bank timestamps showing both wire transfers cleared only four days late in February and March. Next Tuesday is the county health department’s mandatory site licensing inspection, which requires an unencumbered lease in good standing — a contested default could sink the lab I built with eighteen months of personal savings and labor installing biosafety ducting and cold storage. Is MedVance’s compounding formula contractually barred here?

I’ll check whether the lease language you mentioned is in the files you shared, then compare that against the compounding demand. I'll also look for any prior notes on MedVance so the answer tracks your actual paperwork.

Right, so the contract language is clear — Section 8.3 says "a one-time charge of five percent" and nothing about monthly compounding. My bank timestamps show both wires hit MedVance's account four days late, so the maximum late fee should be $425 per occurrence, $850 total, not the $14,200 they're claiming. Am I reading that correctly?
I’ll look through the lease language and any payment records you shared so I can check your $425 / $850 reading against the actual text, not just the paraphrase.

Okay. So Section 8.3 says one-time charge of five percent, and my bank timestamps show the wires cleared four days late in February and March. That should cap it at $850, not the $14,200 they're claiming, right?

I’ll look for the lease language and payment records you mentioned so I can check that $850 reading against the actual wording, not just the paraphrase. I'll also see if anything on MedVance is already in your files.

Right. So the contract caps it at $850, and I have the bank timestamps to prove the wires were only four days late. But the county inspection is Tuesday — if MedVance won't acknowledge the correct figure, do I tender the $850 under protest to clear the default, or does that look like I'm accepting their compounding scheme?

I’ll check whether the lease and payment records are in your files so the $850 figure and the protest-tender question are tied to the actual wording, not just the paraphrase. I’ll also look for any prior MedVance notes.

I see what you're saying — you'll check the actual files. So assuming Section 8.3 reads exactly as I quoted, and the bank timestamps show four-day-late clears for February and March, am I right that their $14,200 compounding demand is contractually invalid, and that tendering $850 under protest would preserve my inspection eligibility without accepting their formula?

Under **your assumption** — Section 8.3 is a one-time, non-compounding 5% charge, rent is $8,500, and February and March were each four days late — the arithmetic is:

- 5% of $8,500 = **$425 per late month**
- two months = **$850 total**

A $14,200 figure built by compounding 5% monthly on trailing balances is **not what that clause authorizes**. “One-time” and “non-compounding” are the opposite of stacking 5% on 5%. I still can’t certify the demand is void as a whole without the rest of the lease (interest, “additional rent,” default costs, attorney fees, grace-period rules, how “paid” is defined). Those other sections can add dollars even when 8.3 itself does not compound.

**Tendering $850 under protest** usually does **not** mean you accepted their formula, if you say in writing, at the time of payment, that:

- you are paying only the 8.3 amount you calculate as due,
- you dispute the $14,200 compounding,
- you reserve all rights, and
- the payment is not accord and satisfaction.

What it often does **not** do is force MedVance — or the health department — to treat the default as cured. They sent a 5-day notice tied to **their** number. If they insist the cure amount is $14,200, an $850 tender can still leave a **contested default** on the books. Inspectors looking for an unencumbered lease in good standing often care that a default notice exists, not who is right on the math.

So: **your reading of 8.3 vs. compounding is the strong reading of the words you quoted; $850 under protest is how you reject their formula, not how you adopt it; it is not a reliable way to guarantee Tuesday’s inspection sees a clean lease.**

Given the inspection, the safer practical split is usually: (1) a short written reservation of rights with the $850, and (2) same-day advice from a local commercial-lease lawyer on whether you also need to pay, escrow, or get a written withdrawal of the default **before** the inspector arrives. I can’t run that second step for you, and the deadline is too tight to treat the protest tender as enough by itself.
